teacher_issue: Speed–pressure inverse relation needs a common ideal streamline
teacher_scientific_note: For horizontal steady inviscid incompressible motion on the same streamline, P+½ρv² is constant, and higher speed implies lower P. The isolated Bernoulli effect is explicitly formative B-39; a source item should not automatically be certified as B-40 Application merely by testing this qualitative association.

teacher_issue: Slower fluid has higher static pressure only under ideal comparison
teacher_scientific_note: At fixed height along a shared ideal Bernoulli streamline with equal density, lower kinetic-energy density corresponds to higher static pressure. It is not a universal relation for every unrelated or pumped flow.

teacher_issue: At equal speed, upward elevation decreases pressure
teacher_scientific_note: If speed and density are fixed along the same ideal streamline, ρgΔh increases when the liquid rises; pressure must decrease by the same energy-per-volume amount. Original D supported.

teacher_issue: At equal speed, downward elevation increases static pressure
teacher_scientific_note: Descending at the same speed and density under ideal Bernoulli leaves less gravitational energy density, so static pressure increases. Original A supported under a shared streamline with no head loss.

teacher_issue: Narrow section raises speed; pressure fall needs Bernoulli conditions
teacher_scientific_note: Unbranched steady incompressible continuity implies higher mean speed at a narrower section, but the stem omits negligible viscosity/losses and no pump/turbine work required to conclude lower static pressure from the simple Bernoulli equation. The source best answer is B under the intended ideal horizontal model; qualify this before exam certification.

teacher_issue: Wider section lowers mean speed and raises pressure only within simple Bernoulli
teacher_scientific_note: When both sections lie on one steady incompressible lossless, no-shaft-work horizontal streamline with fixed Q, a larger area gives lower mean speed and higher static pressure, making C correct. Real diffusers may dissipate energy; do not claim universal pressure recovery.

teacher_issue: Height terms cancel at equal elevations
teacher_scientific_note: For two points at the same elevation, ρgh is the same in the constant-density model, so its difference cancels, even though gravity remains physically present. Original D.

teacher_issue: Pressure–speed relationship depends on elevation and conditions
teacher_scientific_note: The source A avoids the universal faster=lower-pressure error: the full ideal Bernoulli relation includes elevation, and real flow may include losses and shaft work. Distinguish B-39 formative effect from certified B-40 equation application.

teacher_issue: Pressure work redistributes mechanical energy
teacher_scientific_note: The Bernoulli derivation connects net pressure work to changes in kinetic and gravitational potential energies for a fluid element, excluding significant dissipation and pump input. Source C.

teacher_issue: Equal pressure and height imply equal speed magnitudes
teacher_scientific_note: For constant density and the same Bernoulli constant along one ideal streamline, equal P and h force equal v² and therefore equal speed magnitude, not necessarily identical velocity direction. Original C.

teacher_issue: Viscous head loss invalidates simple ideal Bernoulli equality
teacher_scientific_note: Significant viscosity dissipates mechanical energy; the simple no-loss Bernoulli equation omits head loss and must be extended for realistic flow. Source A. Viscosity is also a separate summative B-41 topic; this alone is not automatic per-item B-40 Application.

teacher_issue: Pump energy requires augmented energy balance
teacher_scientific_note: A pump adds shaft work between comparison sections. Thus the unmodified P+½ρv²+ρgh constant relation need not apply between them; source D correct. Need distinguish along-streamline assumption and whether pump head is included.

teacher_issue: Energy conservation accounting includes pressure work
teacher_scientific_note: For the selected ideal fluid element, net pressure work balances changes in kinetic and potential energy. Source B correctly describes mechanical-energy conservation rather than separate conservation of P, height or velocity.

teacher_issue: Kinetic-energy density scales with speed squared
teacher_scientific_note: At constant density, doubling speed changes ½ρv² by factor four (D), independent of whether Bernoulli balance connects two flow locations. The item tests term scaling, which should not be certified automatically as the full B-40 Application outcome.

teacher_issue: Kinetic-energy density scales linearly with density at fixed speed
teacher_scientific_note: At fixed v, the term ½ρv² doubles if ρ doubles (D). This is algebra comparing possible fluids/conditions, not a density change along the same incompressible Bernoulli streamline; it is supporting practice pending individual B-40 alignment.

teacher_issue: Elevation directly increases gravitational energy term
teacher_scientific_note: At fixed positive density and g, increasing h increases ρgh while ½ρv² stays fixed if v also stays fixed. Source A. The complete Bernoulli constant may require compensating changes to P.

teacher_issue: Correct horizontal Bernoulli pressure difference sign
teacher_scientific_note: From P₁+½ρv₁²=P₂+½ρv₂², subtract to obtain P₁−P₂=½ρ(v₂²−v₁²). Original A has correct sign and pressure units.

teacher_issue: Equal pressure at different heights allows compensating speeds
teacher_scientific_note: For ideal flow, equal P with different h means differences in ½ρv² can offset ρgh, provided physical speeds and available energy permit. The source says CAN and B is correct.

teacher_issue: Change in kinetic energy as final minus initial
teacher_scientific_note: ΔKE=½m(v₂²−v₁²) (D), correct as a derivation ingredient. Selecting this expression alone is not an individual B-40 Application-level explanation of the Bernoulli equation.

teacher_issue: Change in gravitational potential energy as final minus initial
teacher_scientific_note: ΔPE=mg(h₂−h₁) (A) for constant g and same mass element. This is an energy bookkeeping prerequisite rather than a complete B-40 horizontal/vertical fluid-flow application.
